\begin{figure}[ht]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{road_network.pdf}
\caption{Benchmark road network as a Markov chain over road nodes (positions in metres). The target drives the edges at 0.03\,m per step and draws its next node on arrival; unlabelled edges have probability 1. At node 4 it picks the north lane (4$\to$5$\to$6, $y{=}{+}0.15$\,m) or the south lane (4$\to$8$\to$9, $y{=}{-}0.15$\,m) with probability 0.5 each. The T-junction (nodes 6 and 9) lies inside occlusion 0, so the turn happens while the target is hidden; it turns the way its lane signals with probability 0.9. These junction occlusions are the 701 exit-prediction events of Tables~\ref{tab:exit-benchmark-tuned} and~\ref{tab:exit-benchmark-shared}, where the lane cue predicts the exit in 638 (91.0\%). Node 1 is a visible 50/50 junction; occlusion 1 covers a straight road with a single exit and is not scored. Right: zoom on the occluded T-junction.}
\label{fig:road-network}
\end{figure}

\par\smallskip\parbox{0.95\linewidth}{\footnotesize Process noise $q$ (per-step position jitter, m) chosen for each particle filter by lowest RMSE all on separate validation runs 100--119 (Table~\ref{tab:noise-sweep-rmse}); DiffPF uses its built-in propagation noise. EnFF (DAFM Ensemble Flow Filter) uses guidance scale $\lambda{=}0.00025$ and path width $\sigma_{\min}{=}0.01$, chosen with its $q$ by the same rule (Table~\ref{tab:enff-sweep}); its constant-velocity forecast plays the role of PF+CV's proposal. PF+TrajFlow, PF+MoFlow and PF+TCFM are ports of the open-source trajectory forecasters trained on the same measurement stream as the other learned models; each particle proposes the first step of one forecast drawn by the method's own mode probabilities. Exit top-1: the side of the box holding the largest share of particle mass, predicting without measurements until 10 steps after the target re-appears, is the side the target exits through; Exit $>$50\%: more than half the mass is beyond that side; $P$(correct exit): mean mass beyond that side. The approach-lane cue predicts the exit in 638/701 (91.0\%) events, the best achievable exit success; chance is 50\%. Runtime measured with 25 benchmark processes sharing the CPU, so it is comparable within this table only. Bold marks the best mean per column, not a statistically significant difference.}
\end{table}
